question.prompt: Let \(S\) be a set of \(6\) integers taken from \(\{1,2,\dots,12\}\) with the property that if \(a\) and \(b\) are elements of \(S\) with \(a < b,\) then \(b\) is not a multiple of \(a.\) What is the least possible value of an element in \(S?\)

solutions.title: Rule out smaller minimum elements
solutions.explanation:
A small element rules out all of its larger multiples. We can use this to show that the least element cannot be \(1\), \(2\), or \(3\).

If \(1\) belongs to \(S\), no other number can belong, since every integer is a multiple of \(1\).

If the least element is \(2\), all larger even numbers are excluded. The only candidates are
\[
\{2,3,5,7,9,11\}.
\]
But \(3\) and \(9\) cannot both be selected, so at most five elements can be chosen.

If the least element is \(3\), the multiples \(6,9,12\) are excluded. The only candidates are
\[
\{3,4,5,7,8,10,11\}.
\]
At most one of \(4,8\) and at most one of \(5,10\) can be selected. These are disjoint pairs, so at least two of the seven candidates must be omitted, again leaving at most five elements.

Thus every valid six-element set has least element at least \(4\). This bound is attained by
\[
S=\{4,6,7,9,10,11\}.
\]
The larger multiples of \(4\) within the allowed range are \(8,12\), and the only larger multiple of \(6\) is \(12\); all are absent. Every other selected number is at least \(7\), so its larger multiples exceed \(12\).

Therefore the least possible value is \(\boxed{4}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
